ZAF.gov: Voters elect a National Assembly, and it chooses the president, who runs the government. There's no separate prime minister. Provinces have their own elected legislatures, and the constitution protects a wide range of rights.
ZAF.vote: Voters choose parties, and seats are shared closely by vote share. In 2024, the ANC lost its majority for the first time since apartheid ended, and formed a national unity government with rivals.
ZAF.history: Dutch and then British settlers took control from the 1600s. From 1910 the government was run by and for the white minority. From 1948 it enforced apartheid, a legal system that kept people apart by race. Decades of resistance and pressure from abroad led to Nelson Mandela's release and the first elections open to all races, in 1994. He became president.

timeline.t: Union of South Africa is formed

NGA.gov: Voters elect a president, who runs the government, along with a National Assembly. Nigeria has 36 states and more people than any other country in Africa, with hundreds of ethnic groups.
NGA.vote: To win, a presidential candidate needs the most votes, plus at least a quarter of the votes in two-thirds of the states, which forces wide national appeal. Disputes over results often go to the courts.
NGA.history: Britain joined its northern and southern lands into one colony in 1914, and Nigeria became independent in 1960. A civil war over the breakaway region of Biafra lasted from 1967 to 1970. Army governments ruled most of the time until 1999, when civilian rule came back.

timeline.t: North and south joined into one colony

EGY.gov: A strong president, backed by the military, holds most of the power. Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has led since 2014, and a 2019 constitutional change lets him stay until 2030. Parliament now has two chambers, the House of Representatives and a Senate added in 2020.
EGY.vote: Elections are held, but critics and rights groups say serious rivals have been jailed or barred. The president has won with roughly 90 to 97 percent. Researchers call Egypt an electoral or closed autocracy, depending on the year. By law everyone must vote, but the fine is rarely enforced.
EGY.history: Army officers overthrew the king in 1952, and military men then led Egypt. The 2011 uprising ended Hosni Mubarak's rule. Mohamed Morsi won the 2012 vote for president, widely seen as the most competitive in Egypt's history. In 2013 the army removed him after mass protests. His supporters called it a coup, and the new leaders called it the people's will.

DZA.gov: A president leads the state, and a prime minister manages government business. Analysts say the army has long held great power behind the scenes. Parliament has two chambers, the People's National Assembly and the Council of the Nation.
DZA.vote: Elections are held, but few people often vote, and critics say tight rules stop real competition. Mass protests in 2019 led long-serving President Abdelaziz Bouteflika to resign.
DZA.history: France invaded Algeria in 1830, and a war from 1954 to 1962 ended French rule. In 1992 the army-backed leaders canceled an election Islamists were about to win. That led to a civil war lasting until about 2002.

timeline.t: Army cancels election; civil war follows

MAR.gov: The king holds the most power, especially over religion, security and foreign affairs. Voters elect a House of Representatives, and the king appoints a head of government from the party with the most seats.
MAR.vote: Parties share out seats in the House of Representatives by their votes, with lists saved for women and young people. Many parties compete. Critics say they govern within limits the palace sets. The monarchy says the 2011 constitution, written after protests, gave parliament and the government real powers. The upper house isn't directly elected.
MAR.history: The Alaouite family has ruled since the 1600s, and Morocco became independent from France and Spain in 1956. Morocco says Western Sahara is part of its land and controls most of it. The Polisario Front and others dispute this.

TUN.gov: President Kais Saied holds huge power. In 2021 he suspended parliament. He called that a lawful answer to a crisis, and opponents called it a self-coup. He then rewrote the constitution to gather power in the presidency. Rights groups say many opponents have been jailed.
TUN.vote: Elections are held, but very few people have voted. Observers and opposition groups say most serious rivals were barred or jailed before the 2024 vote for president, which the president won with over 90 percent.
TUN.history: Tunisia's 2011 revolution removed Zine el-Abidine Ben Ali and began the Arab Spring. For a decade it was the region's one democratic success story. Economic troubles and political deadlock opened the way for Saied.

timeline.t: Ben Ali takes over from Bourguiba

LBY.gov: Libya is split between rival governments. One in Tripoli is recognized by the UN. One in the east is backed by the elected House of Representatives and by military commander Khalifa Haftar. Armed groups hold much of the real power.
LBY.vote: National elections planned for December 2021 were postponed, and have not been held since. The last national parliament, the House of Representatives, was elected in 2014.
LBY.history: Muammar Gaddafi ruled for 42 years after taking power in a 1969 coup. A 2011 uprising, backed by NATO air strikes, ended his rule and he was killed, and Libya has been divided and unstable since.

timeline.t: Gaddafi takes power in a coup
Rival governments emerge, east and west

SDN.gov: Sudan is at war. Since April 2023, the army and a rival force, the RSF, have been fighting for control, and each runs parts of the country. There is no elected government.
SDN.vote: No national elections are being held. The last ones were in 2015, and were widely criticized, and a planned handover to elected rule after the 2019 uprising collapsed.
SDN.history: Independent since 1956, Sudan has seen long civil wars and many coups. South Sudan became a separate country in 2011. Omar al-Bashir ruled from 1989 until the army removed him in April 2019 after months of protests, and the military seized power again in 2021.

timeline.t: Bashir takes power in a coup
War between army and RSF begins

SDS.gov: President Salva Kiir has led since independence in 2011. A 2018 peace deal shares power with his rival, Riek Machar, who was suspended as first vice president in 2025 and put on trial, and the arrangement has often broken down.
SDS.vote: South Sudan has never held a national election as an independent country. They have been postponed five times, and the next is scheduled for 22 December 2026.
SDS.history: After decades of war with the north, South Sudan voted for independence in 2011, becoming the world's newest country. A civil war began just two years later, in 2013, and a peace deal in 2018 ended the main fighting.

timeline.t: Peace deal gives the south autonomy

ETH.gov: Voters elect a House of Peoples' Representatives. The prime minister, who leads the largest party, runs the government. Ethiopia's regions are largely organized around ethnic groups, and the president's job is mostly for show.
ETH.vote: Whoever gets the most votes in each local district wins. The ruling Prosperity Party won a large majority in June 2026, and parts of the country, including all of Tigray, could not vote because of conflict.
ETH.history: Never fully colonized, Ethiopia was ruled by emperors until the military deposed Haile Selassie in 1974 and set up a Marxist government. Rebel forces took power in 1991. Abiy Ahmed won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019, and a war in Tigray followed from 2020 to 2022.

ERI.gov: Isaias Afwerki has led Eritrea since independence in 1993, and only one party, the PFDJ, is legal. A constitution was approved in 1997 but has never been put into effect.
ERI.vote: Eritrea has not held a national election since independence. Rights groups and the UN say many young people are forced into national service with no end date, and that large numbers have fled. The government says the service is needed for defense.
ERI.history: After a 30-year war, Eritrea took control of its own affairs from Ethiopia in 1991 and became officially independent in 1993. A border war with Ethiopia followed, from 1998 to 2000. Critics say the president has tightened control since. The government points to the ongoing threat to its security.

DJI.gov: President Ismail Omar Guelleh has led since 1999, and the constitution's term and age limits have been removed. His party, the RPP, dominates.
DJI.vote: Elections are held, but the opposition has often boycotted, and groups such as Freedom House rate them 'not free'. The president was re-elected in April 2026.
DJI.history: Djibouti was a French colony until 1977. Its port and key location host French, American, Chinese and other military bases.

timeline.t: Guelleh re-elected for a sixth term

SOM.gov: A federal government in Mogadishu faces the armed group al-Shabaab and strong regional states, some of which dispute its power. Clans play a central part in sharing power.
SOM.vote: In the 2022 system, clan elders chose delegates, who elected lawmakers, who elected the president. It rests on clan shares known as the 4.5 formula. A 2024 plan to move to one person, one vote is disputed. Critics say the federal government's terms have been stretched without a vote. The government says that's needed to prepare direct elections.
SOM.history: Siad Barre ruled from a 1969 coup until his government fell in 1991. The country then fell into clan war and famine. A temporary government formed in 2004, and in 2012 came the first lasting federal government since 1991, with help from abroad.

timeline.t: Siad Barre takes power in a coup

SOL.gov: Somaliland runs itself as a separate country, with an elected president and parliament. Its government says it follows on from British Somaliland, while Somalia and most governments treat it as part of Somalia. Israel recognized it in December 2025, the first UN member to do so.
SOL.vote: Voters elect a president and lawmakers, and power has changed hands through voting. Only three parties are allowed at a time. Parliament has a second chamber, the House of Elders, made up of traditional leaders.
SOL.history: Somaliland was a British protectorate. It became independent in June 1960 and joined Somalia days later. After a conflict with Somalia's government, which Somaliland calls a war of independence, it declared its own independence in 1991. Somalia and the African Union don't accept this.

KEN.gov: Voters elect a president, who runs the government, along with a parliament. Since a new constitution in 2010, 47 counties have their own elected governors.
KEN.vote: A president must win over 50% of votes nationally, and at least a quarter of the votes in 24 of the 47 counties. Results are often challenged in court, and the Supreme Court annulled one in 2017.
KEN.history: Kenya won independence from Britain in 1963 and had only one party until the early 1990s. Disputed elections in 2007 led to violence. A power-sharing deal and then the 2010 constitution followed.

timeline.t: Law makes Kenya a one-party state

UGA.gov: Yoweri Museveni has led Uganda since 1986. Limits on a president's terms and age were removed so he could go on, and the army stays deeply involved.
UGA.vote: Many parties compete, but human rights groups say opposition leaders have faced arrest and violence, and observers have doubted results. Museveni was declared the winner in January 2026 with about 72 percent, which critics dispute. Most seats in parliament go by first-past-the-post, and some are set aside for women, the army, young people and others.
UGA.history: Uganda won independence from Britain in 1962. Milton Obote ruled, then Idi Amin after a 1971 coup, then Obote again, and a civil war followed. Museveni's rebels took power in 1986.

timeline.t: Idi Amin takes power in a coup

TZA.gov: A president runs the government. One party, the CCM, and the party it grew from have held power since independence. Zanzibar has its own government within the union.
TZA.vote: The candidate for president with the most votes wins. In the October 2025 election, the two largest opposition parties were barred and foreign observers questioned the vote. Rights groups and others say protests were met with deadly force.
TZA.history: Tanganyika and Zanzibar joined together in 1964. The first president, Julius Nyerere, built a socialist state and a strong national identity. Politics with many parties began in the early 1990s.

RWA.gov: Paul Kagame has held power since 2000 and was the dominant figure before that, as leader of the RPF. A 2015 referendum allows him to stay until 2034. Rwanda is known for strong order and for having the world's highest share of women in parliament.
RWA.vote: Elections are held, but observers and rights groups say the opposition is limited and serious rivals have been barred or jailed. Kagame has won with over 99 percent. The government says this shows his support and the country's recovery.
RWA.history: In 1994, Hutu extremists carried out a genocide, mostly against Tutsi, in about 100 days. Kagame's Tutsi-led rebels ended it. The RPF has ruled since, stressing unity and banning what the law treats as divisive talk about ethnic groups.

BDI.gov: A president runs the government, and the ruling party, the CNDD-FDD, dominates. The constitution shares posts between Hutu and Tutsi.
BDI.vote: Elections are held, but observers and rights groups say the opposition faces tight limits and threats. The main opposition party was in effect shut out of the 2025 vote for parliament. In 2015, the president's bid for a third term set off unrest.
BDI.history: Burundi was a kingdom, then a German and Belgian colony, and became independent in 1962. A coup in 1966 ended the monarchy. Conflict between its Hutu majority and Tutsi minority led to massacres and a civil war from 1993 to 2005.

timeline.t: New constitution shares posts by ethnicity

COD.gov: Voters elect a president and a National Assembly, and provincial assemblies elect the Senate. In the east, armed groups have fought the government for years. They include the M23, which UN experts say Rwanda backs and Rwanda denies.
COD.vote: The president wins with the most votes in one round. Elections have been disputed, and organizing a vote in a huge country with few roads is very hard.
COD.history: Belgium's King Leopold ran the Congo as his own property from 1885, with horrors on a huge scale, until Belgium took it over in 1908. After independence in 1960, its first prime minister, Patrice Lumumba, was killed. Mobutu ruled from 1965 until he was overthrown in 1997. Wars followed from 1996 to 2003.

timeline.t: Belgium takes over from King Leopold

COG.gov: Denis Sassou Nguesso has led for most of the time since 1979, and a 2015 constitutional change let him continue. His party, the Congolese Labour Party, dominates.
COG.vote: Elections are held, but rights groups say opposition figures have been jailed and the internet has been cut during voting. In March 2026 he was announced the winner with about 95 percent, after major opposition parties refused to take part.
COG.history: It won independence from France in 1960, and was a Marxist-Leninist state with one party from 1969. Elections with many parties began in 1992. A civil war in 1997 brought Sassou Nguesso back to power.

CAF.gov: President Faustin-Archange Touadéra runs the government, and a 2023 vote removed term limits. Armed groups hold parts of the country, and Russian military contractors help provide security.
CAF.vote: Elections are held, but violence makes voting impossible in some areas, and the opposition has refused to take part in some. Touadéra won a third term in December 2025 with over 70 percent, while the opposition claimed repression.
CAF.history: It won independence from France in 1960 and has been through many coups. Jean-Bédel Bokassa even declared himself emperor in 1976. Rebels took the capital in 2013, and conflict has driven many people from their homes.

CMR.gov: Paul Biya has been president since 1982, making him one of the world's oldest and longest-serving leaders. Term limits were removed in 2008.
CMR.vote: Elections are held, but opposition groups and observers say leaders have been barred or jailed. Official results gave Biya 54 percent in October 2025. The runner-up disputes that, and there were protests.
CMR.history: It was formed from French and British lands, and became independent in 1960 and 1961. Since 2016, a conflict has gone on between the government and English-speaking separatists.

TCD.gov: Mahamat Déby took over from his father, who was killed fighting rebels in 2021. He first led through a military council, and was declared the winner of a disputed vote for president in 2024.
TCD.vote: Elections are held, but opposition figures say the 2024 vote was unfair. Official results gave Déby 61 percent. A key rival, Yaya Dillo, was killed before it. Officials called that a gun battle, and critics called it an assassination.
TCD.history: Independent from France in 1960, Chad has seen long civil wars and frequent rebellions. Idriss Déby ruled for 30 years, from 1990 to 2021.

NER.gov: The military took power in a July 2023 coup, removing elected President Mohamed Bazoum, who has been detained. The junta has since broken with France and moved closer to Russia.
NER.vote: No elections are planned for now. The junta announced a five-year transition in 2025.
NER.history: Independent from France in 1960, Niger has had several coups. Its 2021 vote was the first peaceful handover of power between elected presidents.

MLI.gov: The military has ruled since coups in 2020 and 2021, led by General Assimi Goïta. It has ended military ties with France and the UN mission, and works with Russian forces.
MLI.vote: Elections have been delayed again and again. Political parties were shut down in 2025. Goïta was given a five-year term that can be renewed, with no election. The junta says that's needed for security and reform.
MLI.history: The ancient Mali Empire was based here. Mali won independence from France in 1960. A 1991 coup led to democracy with many parties. Since 2012, jihadist and Tuareg uprisings have hit the north and center.

BFA.gov: Captain Ibrahim Traoré has ruled since a coup in September 2022, the second that year, while the army fights jihadist groups. Political parties are heavily restricted.
BFA.vote: Promised elections were pushed back, and the transition was extended by five years in 2024.
BFA.history: Revolutionary leader Thomas Sankara renamed the country Burkina Faso in 1984. He was killed in a 1987 coup led by Blaise Compaoré, who ruled until a popular uprising in 2014.

timeline.t: Compaoré takes power in a coup

SEN.gov: A president, elected by voters, has strong powers, and a prime minister helps lead the government. Senegal has never had a successful military coup, which is rare in the region.
SEN.vote: A president needs a majority, or there's a runoff. In 2024, courts and protests blocked an attempt to delay the vote. Opposition candidate Bassirou Diomaye Faye won in the first round.
SEN.history: Independent from France in 1960, Senegal was led by the poet Léopold Senghor. It's seen peaceful handovers of power in 2000, 2012 and 2024.

timeline.t: First handover after an election defeat
Election goes ahead after delay attempt

GMB.gov: Voters elect a president, who runs the government. The country is rebuilding democracy after a long dictatorship.
GMB.vote: Gambians famously vote by dropping marbles into color-coded drums, a method used since the 1960s because many voters couldn't read. Debates continue about whether to keep it.
GMB.history: Independent from Britain in 1965, it was run by Yahya Jammeh from a 1994 coup until 2017. He lost the 2016 election and refused to leave, but left after troops from West African states moved in.

timeline.t: Jammeh takes power in a coup
West African troops help him leave

GNB.gov: Guinea-Bissau has had several coups since independence. The army took power again on 26 November 2025, a day before election results were due. Army leaders now run a temporary government.
GNB.vote: Elections are held, but results have often been disrupted. The November 2025 vote's results were never officially announced because of the coup.
GNB.history: It declared independence from Portugal in 1973 after a long war, and Portugal accepted that in 1974. It has been unstable ever since. UN agencies have called it a stop on the cocaine trade's route.

GIN.gov: Mamady Doumbouya took power in a 2021 coup. He was declared the winner of a December 2025 vote for president, under a new constitution that lets him run. Opposition groups and the UN criticized how the election was run.
GIN.vote: A vote for president was held in December 2025. Opposition groups say major rivals were barred or in exile. The new constitution, approved by voters in September 2025, also adds a Senate.
GIN.history: Guinea alone rejected a French offer of continued ties in 1958, and became independent. Ahmed Sékou Touré then ruled as a one-party state until his death in 1984.

timeline.t: Military takes over after Touré's death

SLE.gov: Voters elect a president, who runs the government, along with a parliament.
SLE.vote: A presidential candidate needs at least 55% of the vote, or else there's a runoff. Results have been disputed, including in 2023.
SLE.history: Founded partly as a home for formerly enslaved people, Sierra Leone became independent from Britain in 1961. A civil war from 1991 to 2002 was partly funded by the sale of diamonds.

timeline.t: Becomes a republic with a president
Multi-party system returns; civil war starts

LBR.gov: Voters directly elect a president, who runs the government. Its system is modelled on that of the United States.
LBR.vote: A president needs a majority, or there's a runoff. In 2023, President George Weah lost and stepped down peacefully.
LBR.history: Freed Black Americans and others founded Liberia and declared independence in 1847. Their descendants held power over the Indigenous majority until a 1980 coup. Two civil wars followed. Ellen Johnson Sirleaf was elected in 2005, the first woman elected to lead an African country.

CIV.gov: A strong president runs the government. Alassane Ouattara won a fourth term in 2025 after courts barred some leading rivals. Critics called that unfair, and officials said it followed the rules.
CIV.vote: A president needs a majority, or there's a runoff. Elections have often been tense, and disputes have turned violent.
CIV.history: Under Félix Houphouët-Boigny, it was stable and well-off for the region for decades after independence from France in 1960. Civil wars followed from 2002 to 2007 and from 2010 to 2011, the second set off by a disputed election.

GHA.gov: Voters elect a president, who runs the government, along with a parliament. Ghana is often called one of Africa's more stable democracies.
GHA.vote: A president needs a majority, or there's a runoff. Parliament uses first-past-the-post. Two main parties have handed power back and forth peacefully, several times.
GHA.history: In 1957, under Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana became the first colony south of the Sahara to win independence. Coups followed, until Jerry Rawlings oversaw a return to rule with many parties in 1992.

TGO.gov: One family has held power since 1967. A 2024 change moved Togo to a parliamentary system, with Faure Gnassingbé taking a new top post, President of the Council of Ministers, which has no term limit.
TGO.vote: Elections are held, but the ruling party dominates. Critics say the new system lets him stay in power with no end date and without facing voters directly.
TGO.history: Gnassingbé Eyadéma took power in a 1967 coup and ruled until he died in 2005. The army then put his son in charge, and a disputed election confirmed him.

timeline.t: Eyadéma takes power in a coup

BEN.gov: Voters elect a president, who runs the government, along with a parliament. Benin was long seen as a model democracy. Critics say rule changes since 2016 have shut out opposition parties, which the government denies.
BEN.vote: A president needs a majority, or there's a runoff. Candidates must gather backing from MPs and mayors, so no major opposition candidate was on the ballot in April 2026. Finance Minister Romuald Wadagni won with over 94 percent, according to official results. International observers said the vote was neither free nor fair.
BEN.history: It was once the Kingdom of Dahomey, and became a Marxist-Leninist state in 1975. In 1990, a national meeting peacefully ended one-party rule. Elections with many parties began in 1991.

MRT.gov: A president, elected by voters, runs the government along with a parliament. Army leaders have played a big part in politics since independence.
MRT.vote: A president needs a majority, or there's a runoff. The 2019 vote was the first handover between two elected presidents, though both were former army generals. The president was re-elected in 2024.
MRT.history: Independent from France in 1960, it has seen several coups. It formally abolished slavery in 1981 and made it a crime in 2007, but rights groups say it persists, and it is often described as the last country to abolish it.

SWZ.gov: King Mswati III is one of the world's last kings with total power. He appoints the prime minister and many lawmakers, and parties can't run in elections.
SWZ.vote: People vote for individual candidates, not parties, through a system based on traditional local councils. Rights groups say pro-democracy protests in 2021 were met with deadly force. The government says it acted to bring back order.
SWZ.history: It was under British protection until independence in 1968, and was called Swaziland until the king renamed it in 2018. King Sobhuza II banned parties in 1973.

timeline.t: Borders drawn by Britain and the Boers

LSO.gov: Voters elect a parliament, and the prime minister runs the government. A king's job is mostly for show. South Africa surrounds Lesotho on all sides.
LSO.vote: A mixed system combines 80 local winners with 40 seats that top up party shares. Coalition governments have often been unstable.
LSO.history: King Moshoeshoe I built the Basotho nation from 1824. Under pressure from Dutch settlers, he accepted British protection in 1868. Lesotho became independent in 1966, and army rule from 1986 ended in 1993.

timeline.t: Moshoeshoe I founds the Basotho nation

BWA.gov: Voters elect a parliament, and it picks the president, who runs the government. Botswana is one of Africa's most stable democracies.
BWA.vote: Whoever gets the most votes in each area wins. In 2024, voters ended one party's 58 years in power, and the president conceded quickly.
BWA.history: Botswana was a very poor British protectorate until independence in 1966. Diamonds, managed with care, then helped it build one of Africa's strongest economies.

timeline.t: Opposition wins for the first time

NAM.gov: A president, elected by voters, runs the government along with a prime minister and a parliament. SWAPO has governed since independence.
NAM.vote: A president needs a majority, or there's a runoff. Parliament's seats are shared by party vote share. In 2024, Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah became the first woman elected president.
NAM.history: Germany made this land a colony in 1884. From 1904 to 1908, German troops carried out a campaign against the Herero and Nama peoples that is widely recognized as a genocide. South Africa then ruled it until independence in 1990.

timeline.t: South Africa given control by League of Nations
UN ends South Africa's mandate; war begins

ZWE.gov: A strong president runs the government. The ZANU-PF party has held power since independence in 1980, and the army plays a big part. In 2026, changes to the constitution were reported to make terms seven years long, with parliament rather than voters choosing future presidents.
ZWE.vote: Elections are held, but observers have reported threats and unfair conditions, which the government rejects. The House of Assembly mixes 210 local winners with 60 extra seats for women, filled by party shares.
ZWE.history: A white minority government declared independence as Rhodesia in 1965, but other countries didn't accept it. After a war, Robert Mugabe led Zimbabwe from 1980 until the army pushed him out in 2017. Some called that a coup, and the army did not.

timeline.t: Amendments extend terms to seven years

ZMB.gov: Voters elect a president, who runs the government, along with a parliament. Zambia has seen several peaceful changes of power since 1991.
ZMB.vote: A president needs over 50%, or there's a runoff. Opposition leader Hakainde Hichilema won in 2021 on his sixth try, and was re-elected in August 2026 with about 60 percent. Observers said the 2026 vote was free and open but not fair, citing use of state money and limits on opposition campaigns. The main challenger disputed the result.
ZMB.history: Zambia won independence from Britain in 1964. Kenneth Kaunda led it until elections with many parties began in 1991, when he lost and stepped down.

MWI.gov: Voters elect a president, who runs the government, along with a parliament.
MWI.vote: A president needs over 50%, or there's a runoff. In 2020, judges threw out a flawed 2019 election and voters changed the result in a rerun, a landmark moment for African courts. In September 2025, the incumbent lost to a former president, Peter Mutharika, and handed over power.
MWI.history: Hastings Banda led from independence from Britain in 1964, first as prime minister and later as president for life. Elections with many parties came in 1994.

timeline.t: Banda makes Malawi a one-party republic

MOZ.gov: A president runs the government, and the Frelimo party has held power since independence.
MOZ.vote: Elections are held, but the opposition and some observers, including the EU, disputed the 2024 result. Many people were killed in the protests that followed.
MOZ.history: Mozambique won independence from Portugal in 1975, then went through a civil war from 1977 until 1992. Elections with many parties began in 1994. An uprising has hit the northern province of Cabo Delgado since 2017.

AGO.gov: The leader of the winning party's list automatically becomes president and has strong powers. The MPLA has governed since independence.
AGO.vote: Voters choose party lists, and seats are shared by vote share. There isn't a separate presidential vote. In 2022 the MPLA won 51 percent and UNITA 44, the closest result in Angola's history, and the opposition challenged the outcome.
AGO.history: Independent from Portugal in 1975, Angola was torn by a 27-year civil war that was also a Cold War battleground, ending in 2002. Critics say oil wealth has been concentrated among a small elite.

timeline.t: MPLA wins by its narrowest margin

GAB.gov: General Brice Oligui Nguema led a 2023 coup that ended the Bongo family's 56-year rule. He won a vote for president in April 2025 under a new constitution.
GAB.vote: A vote for president in April 2025 gave Oligui about 90 percent, with 70 percent of voters reported to have taken part. Term lengths and rules were rewritten in the constitution adopted the year before.
GAB.history: Omar Bongo ruled from 1967 until his death in 2009, when his son took over. Gabon is wealthy from oil but deeply unequal.

GNQ.gov: Teodoro Obiang has ruled since 1979, making him one of the world's longest-serving leaders. His son is vice president, and the PDGE party dominates.
GNQ.vote: Elections are held, but they are described by Freedom House and other observers as neither free nor fair. Obiang wins with over 90 percent, and the opposition has been barred or jailed, according to rights groups.
GNQ.history: It won independence from Spain in 1968. Francisco Macías Nguema, widely described as a brutal dictator, ran it until his nephew Obiang overthrew him in 1979. Large amounts of oil were found in the 1990s.

timeline.t: Macías Nguema declares himself president for life
Obiang overthrows his uncle in a coup

STP.gov: A president, elected by voters, and a prime minister share power. The country has held peaceful, competitive elections.
STP.vote: A president needs a majority, or there's a runoff. The 55-seat National Assembly is elected for four years, with seats shared by party vote share.
STP.history: These islands were a Portuguese colony of big farms, and became independent in 1975. Elections with many parties began in 1991.

CPV.gov: Voters elect a parliament, and the prime minister runs the government. A president, also elected by voters, has a limited role. It's often ranked among Africa's strongest democracies.
CPV.vote: Parliament's 72 seats are shared by party vote share, and the president is elected in two rounds, if needed. Citizens abroad can also vote, in this country with a large diaspora. In May 2026 the opposition PAICV won a majority, unseating the governing MpD.
CPV.history: Nobody lived on the islands until Portuguese settlers came, and they became a base for the slave trade. They won independence in 1975 and held elections with many parties in 1991.

COM.gov: A president runs the government of this island nation. Until 2018 the job moved in turn between the islands. A vote that year ended that, and now a president can serve two five-year terms.
COM.vote: Elections are held, but opposition groups and some observers say they aren't free or fair. In the January 2024 vote for president, official results first gave President Azali about 63 percent. After a review by the Supreme Court, that became about 57 percent.
COM.history: Independent from France since 1975, the Comoros has had more than 20 coups or attempted coups. The island of Mayotte voted in 1974 to remain French and is a French department, but the Comoros still claims it.

timeline.t: Union of the Comoros with island autonomy

MDG.gov: The army took power in October 2025, after young people protested over power and water cuts and an elite army unit joined them. The president left the country and parliament voted to remove him. A colonel now leads a temporary government.
MDG.vote: New elections have been promised, within about two years. The last presidential vote, in 2023, was boycotted by most opposition candidates.
MDG.history: Madagascar won independence from France in 1960. Again and again, protests have brought down its leaders, sometimes with army backing, including in 2009.

timeline.t: Army unit takes power after protests

MUS.gov: Voters elect a parliament, and the prime minister runs the government. A president's job is mostly for show. Mauritius is often ranked among Africa's strongest democracies.
MUS.vote: Each area elects three members, and a small number of 'best loser' seats ensure ethnic balance.
MUS.history: Nobody lived here until Dutch, French and then British colonizers came. Its people come from enslaved Africans and workers brought from India, among others. Mauritius became independent in 1968.

timeline.t: Britain takes the island from France

SYC.gov: A president, elected by voters, runs the government along with a National Assembly.
SYC.vote: A president needs a majority, or there's a runoff. In 2020, an opposition candidate won for the first time since independence. In 2025 the president in office lost a runoff to the main opposition candidate.
SYC.history: Uninhabited until the 1700s, it became independent from Britain in 1976. A coup in 1977 began 16 years of one-party rule.

timeline.t: Opposition wins for the first time

SAH.gov: Morocco controls most of this land and says it's part of Morocco. The Polisario Front, based in refugee camps in Algeria, says it's an independent state, the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, and runs the rest. The UN lists it as a place whose status isn't settled.
SAH.vote: A vote on its future was promised in 1991 but has never been held, because the sides couldn't agree on who may vote. Morocco has offered self-rule under its own control. The Polisario wants a vote that includes independence.
SAH.history: Spain left its colony in 1975. Morocco and Mauritania moved in, setting off a war with the Polisario Front. Mauritania pulled out in 1979, and a ceasefire watched over by the UN began in 1991.

timeline.t: Spain leaves; Morocco and Mauritania move in
